analysis.one_liner: Requires a 10-cent refundable deposit on beer and soda containers, with unclaimed deposits funding state recycling.
analysis.headline: The national bottle-deposit bill, introduced by one senator with one cosponsor, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every beer, soda, mineral water, and wine cooler container sold nationwide to carry a 10-cent refund value. Consumers could get the money back by returning empty containers, and unclaimed deposits would flow to state governments each year to pay for recycling and pollution-prevention programs. It would also ban pull-tab metal cans and forbid distributors and retailers from dumping container materials in landfills.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who return containers get their deposit back, plus at least a 2-cent handling bonus when redeeming through a distributor. States receive unclaimed deposits for recycling programs. Communities gain from less litter and lower waste-disposal costs, which the bill's findings say currently fall on local governments, private businesses, farmers, and landowners. People who collect cans for income — often those with the least money — would get a guaranteed redemption price nationwide.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, state recycling programs, and communities

how_it_helps.text: Every beer, malt beverage, mineral water, soda water, wine cooler, and carbonated soft drink container would carry a 10-cent refund value that consumers recover by returning the empty container to a retailer or distributor selling that brand and size.
Distributors must pay at least 2 cents per container above the deposit to anyone redeeming containers through them, directly compensating the people who do the collecting.

Each year, distributors must hand over unclaimed deposits to state governments, which must use the money for pollution prevention and recycling programs — a funding stream the bill says communities otherwise struggle to raise.

The bill's findings state that container litter and solid waste impose collection and disposal costs on public agencies, private businesses, farmers, and landowners, and that state deposit laws have proven inexpensive to administer while shifting recycling and litter costs onto beverage producers and consumers.
The bill bans metal cans with parts that detach when opened (pull-tabs) and prohibits retailers and distributors from landfilling beverage containers or their metal, glass, or plastic.

States that already run comparable deposit laws, or that show they recycle or reuse at least 70 percent of beverage containers, are exempt from the federal requirements, preserving stronger state systems.

analysis.who_pays: Beverage distributors bear the heaviest costs: collecting the deposit from retailers, paying refunds plus at least 2 cents handling on every returned container, paying unclaimed deposits to states annually, and keeping container materials out of landfills. Retailers must collect deposits from customers, store and redeem empties, and face up to $1,000 in civil penalties per violation. Some of these compliance costs would likely reach consumers through beverage prices, and consumers who never return containers forfeit their deposits to state recycling funds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Beverage distributors, retailers, and non-redeeming consumers

drawbacks.text: Consumers pay the 10 cents up front on every covered drink, and anyone who does not bother to return containers loses that money permanently — the bill routes those forfeited deposits to state governments rather than back to the buyer.

Retailers must collect and hold deposits, take back used containers, and store the empties on site, which adds handling work, storage space, and sanitation burdens to every store that sells beer or soda.

Distributors face annual accounting and payment obligations to every state, plus civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation for misreporting unclaimed refunds, and those administrative costs would tend to be passed into drink prices.
The 10-cent refund value only adjusts for inflation every 10 years, so the real value of the incentive would erode between adjustments.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but narrow: an up-front deposit that is recoverable, and handling and paperwork burdens on beverage companies and stores. The gains are broad — cleaner communities, lower waste-disposal costs for local governments and landowners, a new funding stream for state recycling programs, and a guaranteed per-can payment for anyone who collects containers. The bill itself cites state deposit laws as inexpensive to administer and effective. On balance the design is straightforward and the costs fall mostly on the industry that creates the containers, though the forfeited deposits of non-redeeming consumers function as a small tax on them.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Hatfield of Oregon introduced the bill on May 26, 1995, for himself and Senator Jim Jeffords of Vermont.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation — the standard first step for a bill.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote. The action history ends with the referral, and the bill expired when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Beverage distributors and retailers came out ahead: a national deposit-and-redemption system never arrived, so they avoided its collection, handling, and reporting costs. Consumers and states lost the refunds and recycling funding the bill would have created.

for.name: Sen. Mark Hatfield
for.role: U.S. Senator from Oregon; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Beverage Container Reuse and Recycling Act of 1995 and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: Sen. Jim Jeffords
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; sole cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, joining Hatfield at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (chaired by Sen. Larry Pressler)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 26, 1995 and never reported it out, held no recorded hearing or markup, and never sent it to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the only cosponsor were Republicans, and the bill never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Beverage distributors (beer, soft drinks, wine coolers)
industries.note: Distributors would have to collect the 10-cent deposit from retailers, pay refunds plus at least 2 cents handling on every container returned through them, pay unclaimed deposits to states annually, and keep container materials out of landfills. This shifts the cost of litter and recycling — currently borne by towns and landowners — onto the beverage trade, which is why deposit systems have long faced industry resistance.

industries.industry: Grocery, convenience, and other beverage retailers
industries.note: Retailers would have to charge the deposit on every covered drink, take back and pay refunds on used containers, store the empties, and face civil penalties for violations. The redeem-at-any-store-selling-that-brand rule spreads redemption work across all sellers rather than concentrating it at return centers.

The bill bans metal cans with parts that detach when opened, forcing design changes, and its ban on landfilling container metal reinforces a recycling stream the industry must supply rather than discard.

States would receive annual unclaimed-deposit payments earmarked for pollution prevention and recycling, and communities would bear less of the cost of collecting littered containers and disposing of container waste.
